metadata.title: LearningO - English / Listen
metadata.subject: English
metadata.generated_for: Children with dyslexia and other learning differences, approx. ages 5-10
design_principles: Every question is answerable without reading. Audio carries the load, emoji carry the meaning.
Instructions are five to eight words, one clause, present tense.
Target words are decodable or high-frequency, and are themselves useful life-skill vocabulary (soap, help, wait, share, bin, tap, kind).
Every question teaches something about real life while it tests a listening skill, so the practice doubles as quiet life coaching.
Three difficulty bands rotate inside every type: easy for fluency, medium for growth, happy for joy. A child never meets more than two hard items in a row.
Wrong options are never random. Each one is a specific, named misconception, so a single wrong tap becomes a diagnosis.
Feedback praises the process, never the child's intelligence, to protect self-belief over the long run.
Safety, honesty and help-seeking items carry a mastery_weight above 1.0 so they surface in reports even when accuracy overall is high.

tts_guidance.note: Read audio_text exactly as written. For sequence and multi-select items, pause 500ms between listed items.

question_type_registry.primary_construct: spoken word to written word matching
question_type_registry.diagnostic_purpose: Can the child hold a spoken word and pick its exact written form from near-identical choices?
Does the child know the meaning of the everyday word, separate from reading it?
Can the child judge a whole spoken sentence against what they know about the world?
Rhyme is the earliest reliable predictor of reading. Weakness here explains later decoding trouble.
Links a heard sound to a letter shape. This is the core skill dyslexia disrupts.
Children who drop word endings in speech also drop them in spelling. This finds it early.
Syllable control is how long words become readable. Weakness shows up as guessing at long words.

question_type_registry.primary_construct: holding three items and comparing them
question_type_registry.diagnostic_purpose: Needs all three words held in mind at once. A clean window into auditory working memory.
Good readers guess from context. This measures that strategy with no reading load.

question_type_registry.primary_construct: temporal sequencing of a real-life routine
question_type_registry.diagnostic_purpose: Sequencing weakness is a core dyslexia signature and also predicts trouble getting ready on time.

question_type_registry.primary_construct: holding several spoken words while matching
question_type_registry.diagnostic_purpose: Three pairs at once shows how the child copes when listening load rises.

question_type_registry.primary_construct: selecting several targets while rejecting a tempting one
question_type_registry.diagnostic_purpose: Stopping after one answer is an impulse signal. Adding a wrong one is a filtering signal.

question_type_registry.primary_construct: multi-step spoken instruction with a temptation to ignore
question_type_registry.diagnostic_purpose: The single best classroom-behaviour predictor in the whole bank. Also measures impulse control.

question_type_registry.primary_construct: social and safety judgement from a short spoken scenario
question_type_registry.diagnostic_purpose: Shows the child's real-world decision instincts, not just their listening.

question_type_registry.primary_construct: drawing a conclusion the story never states
question_type_registry.diagnostic_purpose: The highest-value question type. Strong inference with weak decoding is the classic dyslexic profile, and finding it protects the child's self-belief.

difficulty_band.easy: Consolidation. Child should succeed ~90% of the time. Builds fluency and confidence.
difficulty_band.medium: Learning edge. Target ~65-75% success. This is where growth data lives.
difficulty_band.happy: Pure joy question. Near-certain success, silly or warm content, low mastery weight. Placed to reset mood after effort and to keep the session feeling like play.

reporting_recipes.skill_profile: Group accuracy by academic.skill and cognition.process to find the child's cognitive shape (e.g. strong discriminate / weak sequence).
reporting_recipes.life_skill_radar: Group accuracy by life_skill.domain across all subjects to build a 14-spoke life-skill radar chart per child.
reporting_recipes.dyslexia_error_map: Count wrong answers by distractor_insight value, not just by question. The distractor tells you WHY, so one wrong tap becomes a diagnosis.
reporting_recipes.attention_curve: Plot time_to_first_touch and accuracy against telemetry.session_position to find the child's real attention span, then cap session length there.
reporting_recipes.working_memory_ceiling: Accuracy vs cognition.working_memory_load. The load level where accuracy drops below 60% is the child's current WM ceiling - never exceed it during teaching.
reporting_recipes.confidence_calibration: Compare the wellbeing.confidence_prompt answer with actual correctness. Confident+wrong = misconception to correct. Unsure+right = needs reassurance, not more teaching.
reporting_recipes.impulsivity_index: Wrong answers where time_to_first_touch < 25% of expected_response_time_ms. High index means teach 'wait and think', not more content.
reporting_recipes.persistence_index: Retry rate and abandon rate on medium-band items. Falling persistence over weeks is an early wellbeing flag.
reporting_recipes.mood_trend: Track emotion_checkin responses over sessions. Two sad check-ins in a row should lower difficulty automatically for the next session.
reporting_recipes.personality_map: Aggregate personality_signal outcomes to describe tendencies (e.g. cautious, highly pro-social, low help-seeking) for the parent report.

wellbeing_rules: No question ever shows a countdown clock. Speed is rewarded, never punished.
Feedback praises the process ('you listened right to the end'), never the child's intelligence.
After two wrong answers the app shows how it works instead of asking again.
A happy-band question follows any run of three errors.
Every safety and help-seeking question points the child towards a trusted grown-up.
